To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) ecosystem respiration was lower and temperature sensitivity was greater in communities with permafost than in communities without permafost, and 2) the apparent temperature sensitivity of ecosystem respiration was negatively related to the water table position, suggesting that respiration in wetlands with saturated soil conditions is oxygen-limited and not strongly influenced by temperature.

(1) Ecosystem respiration (ER), the sum of autotrophic and heterotrophic respiration, is temperature-limited in most wetland vegetation communities, but is oxygen-limited in the most waterlogged communities; (2) The contribution of root respiration to ER was 40% in two communities that differed significantly in their rates of ER; and (3) ER was more sensitive to temperature under drier soil moisture conditions.

(1) the apparent Q10 for monthly averaged ER was lower in drier communities, (2) root respiration contributed similarly to ER across a wetland gradient despite differences in root respriration rates, and (3) ER was more related to root biomass in wet communities with low redox conditions, and more related to green area and vascular plant biomass in drier communities.
